extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of public management, communications, and persuasion (e.g., public managers, policy communicators, PR professionals)
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes Robert Cialdini’s six principles of influence and provides examples of how each operates in real-world persuasion and marketing contexts. Useful for designing persuasive communications, campaigns, or public-management messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocity
rubrics_metrics.description: People tend to return a favor, thus the pervasiveness of free samples in marketing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and notes from the page: Ethiopia providing thousands of dollars in humanitarian aid to Mexico after the 1985 earthquake (reciprocating earlier diplomatic support), and the good cop/bad cop strategy are given as illustrations. Use small favors or gifts to trigger a sense of obligation to reciprocate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scarcity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Saying offers are available for a 'limited time only' encourages sales. Guidance: emphasize limited availability, rarity, or time-limited opportunities to increase perceived value and urgency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority
rubrics_metrics.description: People will tend to obey authority figures, even if they are asked to perform objectionable acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and cautionary notes: Cites the Milgram experiments and the My Lai massacre as demonstrations of obedience to authority. Guidance implies leveraging credible expertise or authoritative endorsement increases compliance, but be mindful of ethical implications and potential misuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: If people commit, orally or in writing, to an idea or goal, they are more likely to honor that commitment because of establishing that idea or goal as being congruent with their self-image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes and examples: Once people agree, they often continue to honor the agreement even if initial incentives are removed; references cognitive dissonance and Cialdini's note about Chinese brainwashing of American POWs to rewrite self-image and gain automatic unenforced compliance. Guidance: obtain small initial commitments (verbal or written) to increase later compliance; be aware of ethical concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liking
rubrics_metrics.description: People are easily persuaded by other people that they like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Tupperware marketing—people were more likely to buy if they liked the person selling it. Also notes biases favoring more attractive people (physical attractiveness stereotype). Guidance: increase affinity, similarity, or attractiveness of messengers to improve persuasive effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: People will do things that they see other people are doing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example experiment: Confederates looking up into the sky induced bystanders to look up as well, at one point stopping traffic; references conformity and the Asch conformity experiments. Guidance: use social proof (demonstrating others' behavior or approval) to encourage adoption, but be careful about accuracy and ethical presentation of social data.
